description_full: Carrier Global Corporation provides intelligent climate and energy solutions in the United States, Europe, the Asia Pacific, and internationally. It operates through four segments: Climate Solutions Americas; Climate Solutions Europe; Climate Solutions Asia Pacific, Middle East & Africa; and Climate Solutions Transportation. The company provides air conditioners, heating systems, heat pumps, home and building energy management systems, automation systems, aftermarket components, and repair and maintenance and rental services, as well as modernization and upgrades to meet the heating, cooling, and ventilation needs of residential and commercial customers. It also offers transport refrigeration and monitoring products, services, and digital solutions for trucks, trailers, shipping containers, and intermodal and rail applications. The company offers its products under the Carrier, Viessmann, Toshiba, Automated Logic, Bryant, CIAT, Day & Night, Heil, NORESCO, Carrier Transicold, and Sensitech brands. The company was incorporated in 2019 and is headquartered in Palm Beach Gardens, Florida.

financial_summary: Carrier Global Corporation is a large-cap industrials business with a $42.9B market cap on $21.7B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +2% over the past three years, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 12% against a 9% cost of capital, a 3-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it.

The business throws off $2.1B in free cash flow — roughly 10 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.69× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 3.0× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 4.7×.
Management returns a meaningful 8.5% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 4.8% of the shares.

sect: Its 10% operating margin is roughly in line with the Industrials median (9%).
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.91x).

The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 544 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are roughly flat over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 32% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 35% and a beta of 1.19, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.71 vs 5y 1.23), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $311.7M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 25% in the 2020 crash and 36% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $45.82 (margin of safety -14%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 43%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $34.25 to $62.40 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Multiples send mixed signals against Industrials peers: cheaper on P/E 16.4 vs 23.3, richer on EV/EBITDA 16.7 vs 13.3 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 14% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 4.9% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 4.0% (vs the 8% bar).
The 23 covering analysts target $68.79 on average, 31% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 12% earns above the cost of capital of 9.1%, but the 3pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.52).
It converts 10% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.69x.
ROE of 11% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.7x equity multiplier).
It spends 2.9% of revenue on R&D and 0.3% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 3.0x net debt to EBITDA ($1.6B of cash against $11.8B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 4.7x.
Goodwill makes up 42% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 2.1% over 3 years and 4.5% over 5 years, so growth is decelerating.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 9.0% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a backlog worth 31% of annual revenue and deferred revenue up 25%.
Capex runs only 0.3x depreciation (1.8% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
own: Insiders own a modest 4.8%, and institutions hold 91%.
It returns 8.5% a year to shareholders (6.7% in buybacks and 1.8% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 0.7% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
people: With about 47,000 employees, each generates about $463K of revenue, 1.3x the Industrials median, and productivity has risen 4.5% a year.
That works out to $45K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $3.3M (7x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores poorly (9/10, lower is better).
